A Design Bible in Progress

Every song is
a creature with eyes.

Soundgarden is an infinite, Mercator-projected canvas where every song grows into a living thing — watching, breathing, and becoming more itself each time someone listens. This page is a sketch of what those creatures look like and the six worlds they grow inside.

First Principles

Four things we won't compromise on.

Everything else is a moving target. These are the load-bearing ones.

01

They look back at you.

Every creature has eyes. Not decoration — the primary read. Eyes track your cursor, blink, drift, sleep. A single glance at the canvas should feel like being watched by a hundred quiet beings.

02

The visual is the music.

Complexity is composition complexity. Size is reach. Tentacles are collaborators. Pulse is tempo. You don't need to hear a creature to know how it sounds — you can read it like sheet music made of light.

03

One cosmos, six states.

No jungles. No reefs. Soundgarden is a single dark canvas, and each region is a musical state of being — Drift, Pulse, Fracture, Swing, Hush, Grid. Biomes are moods, not ecosystems.

04

Born in real places.

The canvas is a Mercator projection of Earth. Lagos sounds like Lagos because Lagos is there. Chart-seeded organisms are the wild flora; user-planted ones are cultivated guests. Real coordinates, real cultures, real colour.

Part One / The Six States

Six states of music, not six places.

Each state is a mood the world can be in — a way music exists. Every state below shows two creature archetypes across four life stages: seed · sprout · bloom · ancient.

Part Two / A Life in Four Moments

A creature is a chronicle.

Stage is not scale. A seed has one closed eye. A sprout opens one eye and grows a tentative limb. A bloom is at peak life. An ancient is lopsided, many-eyed, surrounded by offspring, half-fossilised and twice as bright.

Growth by engagement

New contributors add limbs. Plays open new eyes. Forks introduce asymmetric mutations that never go away. An ancient is a record of everyone who ever touched it.

Decay & legacy

Dormancy dims the body but the silhouette remains. Creatures that outlive their contributors fossilise into mycelium — permanent ground features that shape what grows nearby.

Part Three / Open Questions

The things we still need to decide.

Not blockers. Fork points. Each one opens a different version of the product.

Q.01
How do wild and cultivated creatures differ at a glance?
Chart-seeded organisms could have a distinct eye shape — slit pupils, or multiple rings of iris — marking them as grown, not planted. Cultivated ones show the hand of their maker. Or the difference is metadata only.
Q.02
Is the globe a portal, or a persistent second view?
Option A: globe is the landing screen and vanishes once you dive in. Option B: a mini-globe always floats in the corner, spinning, with live activity pips. B is more alive but adds chrome.
Q.03
Does the garden make sound on its own?
If every creature is music, the canvas is technically a symphony. Do we render ambient audio from nearby organisms (risk: cacophony)? Or is the world silent until you focus on a single creature?
Q.04
"Now Boarding" — literal split-flap, or just the pattern?
A departure board on the landing page is a beautiful image. But it's also a specific aesthetic that might fight the canvas. Do we commit to the literal board, or keep only the interaction — jump to trending regions?
Q.05
Do cultural palettes change anatomy, or just colour?
Tinting Reykjavík cool and Lagos warm is easy and probably good. Letting regions have entirely different creature anatomies is harder, riskier, and potentially far more interesting.
Q.06
What does an eye do when it's bored?
Cursor tracking is obvious. But what about idle behaviour? Do eyes close? Drift? Watch each other? This is a small question with enormous consequences for how alive the canvas feels.
